Botticelli. Sandro Botticelli (1445-1510) was a Florentine painter whose elegant, decorative style defined the early Italian Renaissance. He is immortalised for two paintings-The Birth of Venus and Primavera-that revolutionised how Renaissance artists depicted beauty, mythology, and divine grace. Though he worked alongside Leonardo and Michelangelo, his influence operated through a distinctly different aesthetic: flowing lines, ethereal figures, and a spiritual intensity that made him a favourite of the ruling Medici family and the intellectual circles of Florence. Born in Florence in 1445 as Alessandro di Mariano Filipepi; "Botticelli" was a nickname derived from his goldsmith brother's surname. In addition, apprenticed under Filippo Lippi and later worked in the workshop of Verrocchio, the same master who trained Leonardo da Vinci, absorbing the technical foundations of Renaissance art. Similarly, painted The Birth of Venus (circa 1484-1486), an iconic tempera panel showing the goddess emerging from the sea on a shell, her golden hair and serene face epitomising Renaissance idealised beauty. Another important aspect is that created Primavera (circa 1477-1482), an allegorical scene of spring with dancing figures and flowing drapery that captured the optimism and classical learning of the Medici court. It's also worth knowing that developed a distinctive linear style emphasising flowing contours and rhythmic movement rather than the sculptural solidity favoured by Michelangelo or the optical realism pioneered by Leonardo. Also worth noting is that received major commissions from the Medici family, for whom he executed both secular mythologies and sacred altarpieces, cementing his position as Florence's court painter. In addition, shifted his later work toward religious subjects, particularly scenes of the Virgin Mary, reflecting both personal piety and the rise of the Dominican friar Savonarola's moral influence over Florence. Finally, executed The Temptation of Saint Jerome and other devotional works that showed deeper psychological drama, moving beyond the decorative surface of his mythological paintings.
